profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-industry design review is being held to evaluate the near-final outline and evidence table for a review paper titled 'Robotic Infrastructure Inspection Systems' that will be submitted to a civil engineering journal. The paper synthesizes studies on robots used for bridge, tunnel, pipe, and building inspections, with emphasis on the tradeoff between mobility and sensing, the rise of NDE payloads, and future challenges in autonomy and data handling. The agenda is to review whether the current draft structure, comparison tables, and screening decisions are ready for final polishing, and to decide what revisions are needed before sending the manuscript to co-authors. The expected outcome is agreement on whether the review package is 'submission-ready' and what final edits will be made to the taxonomy, evidence summaries, and challenge section.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Lead Review Author and Associate Professor of Civil Infrastructure Systems
members.expertise: Infrastructure inspection, nondestructive evaluation, review synthesis, bridge and tunnel asset management
members.background: Lena leads an academic lab on digital inspection methods and has coordinated several literature reviews for civil engineering journals; she is responsible for the manuscript narrative, inclusion logic, and alignment with infrastructure practice.
members.private_state: She wants the paper to feel comprehensive to civil engineering readers without reopening major restructuring, and is especially concerned that the review preserve practical distinctions between field-deployed inspection systems and laboratory robotics demonstrations.
hidden_assumptions: A 'commercially available robotic system' can still count as such in the review even if the inspection payload and field adaptation were research-customized, because the base mobility platform is what matters for the review trend.
A paper is 'ready for submission' once the argument, taxonomy, and representative evidence are stable, even if citation formatting, figure harmonization, and a few table cells remain for cleanup.
The 'screened corpus' refers to studies that survived full-text eligibility for synthesis in the main comparative tables, not every paper captured in the broader search log.

When the paper says 'inspection-driven autonomy,' it mainly means autonomy that supports inspection coverage and decision support in realistic field settings, not merely local navigation capability shown in controlled experiments.

members.name: Evan Park
members.role: Robotics Systems Engineer and Industry Co-author
members.expertise: Mobile robotics integration, autonomous navigation, sensor payload packaging, industrial deployment pathways
members.background: Evan works at an engineering robotics firm that adapts UAVs, crawlers, and climbing robots for industrial inspection pilots; he brings a systems-integration perspective and has been helping standardize the paper's classification tables and deployment claims.
members.private_state: He wants the review to look methodologically tidy and technically current, and is trying to avoid reviewer criticism that the paper overstates maturity or mixes prototype demonstrations with deployable systems.
hidden_assumptions: A 'commercially available robotic system' should only be labeled that way if the inspection configuration discussed in the paper was available as an off-the-shelf package rather than a custom research integration built on a commercial base.

A manuscript is 'ready for submission' only when tables, references, figure labels, and category definitions are fully normalized, because those details determine whether reviewers see the review as rigorous.

The 'screened corpus' refers to the entire set of papers that passed abstract screening and therefore should remain traceable in counts and appendix summaries even if some are not discussed in the main tables.

When the paper mentions 'inspection-driven autonomy,' it should include robots that autonomously execute coverage paths or local sensing routines, even in constrained testbeds, because these are valid autonomy precursors for practice.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a commercially available system
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the section on the 'expanded use of commercially available robotic systems.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means systems whose locomotion platform is commercially sold, even if the sensing stack, mounting, and inspection workflow were heavily customized by researchers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means end-to-end inspection configurations that were available off the shelf or near-commercial in the exact form used, excluding most research-customized integrations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to shorthand references to 'commercial platforms' and neither expects the other to distinguish between the base robot and the complete inspection package during a high-level review discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the draft is almost 'ready for submission' after a few final edits.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the conceptual structure and substantive claims are stable enough to circulate for approval, with minor formatting and table completion handled in parallel.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the manuscript should not be called ready until cross-references, classification consistency, table completeness, and reference normalization are all fully closed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In review meetings, 'ready' is commonly used as a broad progress label, and both assume the other shares their normal publication standard without needing to spell out the threshold.

misalignment_points.topic: Which papers are included in the screened set
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether 'the screened set' adequately supports the comparison table and challenge section.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the narrower full-text eligible studies that appear in the synthesis tables and narrative analysis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the larger post-abstract-screening pool that should still anchor counts, exclusions, and appendix traceability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have worked with multiple intermediate literature pools and casually use the same label because each regards their own reference set as the obvious default at this stage.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of autonomy examples in the future challenges section
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to strengthen the discussion of 'inspection-driven autonomy' as an outstanding challenge.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the section should focus on autonomy demonstrated in realistic infrastructure inspection contexts, such as coverage planning around actual defects, field constraints, or asset-management integration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the section can also draw on constrained pilot studies where robots autonomously navigate or collect data in mockups, because those studies are still relevant stepping stones for inspection autonomy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds specific enough to imply shared meaning, and both see testbed work as related to practice, so the boundary of what belongs in the challenge discussion never gets explicitly negotiated.

To me, we're almost ready for submission because the narrative arc, taxonomy, and evidence base are stable; the remaining issues are cleanup items like figure alignment, citation formatting, and a few table cells.
